title: Ser, estar and how you feel
objectives: I can ask and answer Como você está? and say how I feel.
I can explain why estou, está, estão, simpático and similar words are spelled and stressed the way they are.
I can describe people with adjectives that agree in gender and number.

vocabulary.note: The second Portuguese verb for to be. Ser says what something is; estar says where it is and what condition it is in at the moment. It comes from Latin stare, to stand. Es-TAR ends in r, so by the default rule the stress is on the last syllable and no accent is needed. The present forms are estou, está, estamos and estão.

Feminine: cansada. The an before s ends a syllable, so the a is nasal: kan-SA-du, with the final o said u. The stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for a word ending in o, so there is no accent.

Same form for men and women; plural: felizes. A word ending in z is stressed on the last syllable by default (fe-LIZ), so no accent is needed. The final z is said s in São Paulo and sh in Rio; in felizes the z sits between vowels and is said z.
Same form for men and women. The final e is weak and said i, so the t before it is said tch: TRIS-tchi. The tr is a tap, as in prato.

An adverb, so it never changes for gender or number: men and women both say Estou bem. Final em is a nasal vowel, said like ayn through the nose, and the lips do not close for the m. Estou bem is the standard way to say you are fine.
The opposite of bem and also an adverb, so it never changes. With estar it means unwell. The l at the end of a syllable is said w, so mal is said MAW, like the start of English mouse.

Portuguese names the feeling with a noun: you are with hunger, where English uses the adjective hungry. Because fome is a noun, it never changes for gender: Ela está com fome. Always estar, never ser. The o of fome is closed and the final e is said i: FO-mi.
Sono is the noun sleep, so there is no agreement. In com the m only nasalizes the o and the lips do not close: kõ. The stressed o of sono is closed: SO-nu.
Sede is a noun, so there is no agreement. The d comes before the weak final e, which is said i, so the d is said dj: SE-dji, with a closed e.

Same form for men and women. Oe is two strong vowels side by side, which never form a diphthong, so the word has three syllables: do-EN-te. The en before t is nasal and the t before the final e is said tch.
Feminine: ocupada. The c before u is said k: o-ku-PA-du. The stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for a word ending in o.
Feminine: alta. The l at the end of a syllable is said w: AW-tu. Used with ser, because height is part of what a person is.

dialogues.title: How are you today?
dialogues.context: Ana and Carlos meet in the street near the hospital. Ana is in the middle of a long day at work.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.target: Oi, Carlos! Como você está?
lines.source: Hi, Carlos! How are you?

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.target: Oi, Ana! Estou bem, obrigado. E você?
lines.source: Hi, Ana! I am fine, thank you. And you?
lines.source_literal: Hi, Ana! I-am well, obliged. And you?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.target: Estou muito cansada. Estou com sono.
lines.source: I am very tired. I am sleepy.
lines.source_literal: I-am very tired. I-am with sleep.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.target: Você está ocupada hoje?
lines.source: Are you busy today?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.target: Estou, sim. Sou enfermeira e estou no hospital hoje.
lines.source: Yes, I am. I am a nurse and I am at the hospital today.
lines.source_literal: I-am, yes. I-am nurse and I-am in-the hospital today.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.target: Enfermeira? Que legal! Eu sou professor.
lines.source: A nurse? How cool! I am a teacher.
lines.source_literal: Nurse? What cool! I am teacher.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.target: Professor? Você não é engenheiro?
lines.source: A teacher? Aren't you an engineer?

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.target: Não, eu não sou engenheiro. Sou professor.
lines.source: No, I am not an engineer. I am a teacher.
lines.source_literal: No, I not am engineer. I-am teacher.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.target: Desculpa, Carlos! Hoje estou muito cansada.
lines.source: Sorry, Carlos! Today I am very tired.
lines.source_literal: Excuse, Carlos! Today I-am very tired.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.target: Tudo bem, Ana. Até logo!
lines.source: That's fine, Ana. See you later!

dialogues.title: Who is that?
dialogues.context: Pedro and Marina are at a party. Pedro asks Marina about two people he does not know.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.target: Marina, quem é ele?
lines.source: Marina, who is he?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: Ele é o Rafael, um amigo.
lines.source: He is Rafael, a friend.
lines.source_literal: He is the Rafael, a friend.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.target: Ele é engenheiro?
lines.source: Is he an engineer?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: É, sim. E é muito simpático e engraçado.
lines.source: Yes, he is. And he is very nice and funny.
lines.source_literal: Is, yes. And is very nice and funny.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.target: E ela? Quem é ela?
lines.source: And her? Who is she?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: Ela é a Paula. Ela é médica.
lines.source: She is Paula. She is a doctor.
lines.source_literal: She is the Paula. She is doctor.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.target: Ela é muito bonita! E alta.
lines.source: She is very pretty! And tall.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: É, e é muito inteligente também.
lines.source: Yes, and she is very intelligent too.
lines.source_literal: Is, and is very intelligent too.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.target: Onde ela está?
lines.source: Where is she?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.target: Ela está aqui, com o Rafael.
lines.source: She is here, with Rafael.
lines.source_literal: She is here, with the Rafael.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: reading the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Every word in this unit can be read with the rules from the first three lessons. Nothing here needs a new rule, only practice in applying the old ones, and the lesson is easier if you do the same four steps every time. First, divide the word into syllables. Second, find the stressed syllable by ear. Third, read the default stress from the ending: a word ending in a, e or o (with or without a final s), am, em or ens is stressed on the second to last syllable, and a word ending in anything else is stressed on the last syllable. Fourth, if the real stress breaks the default, the stressed vowel carries a written accent, acute for an open vowel and circumflex for a closed one. Then read each letter by the sound rules: a final unstressed o is said u and a final unstressed e is said i; t and d before the sound i become tch and dj; l at the end of a syllable is w; a vowel followed by an m or n that ends the syllable is nasal; h is silent.

The forms of estar are the best practice, because the same rules explain every accent and tilde on them. Estar is es-TAR. It ends in r, so the default is the last syllable and no accent is needed. Estou is es-TOW: ou is a diphthong, which is one syllable, and the default for a diphthong ending is the last syllable, so again no accent. Está is es-TÁ: it ends in a, so the default would be ES-ta, but the stress is on the last syllable, so the stressed vowel is marked, and acute because the a is open. That one accent is the only difference between está (is) and esta (this, said ES-ta). Estamos ends in os, so it is stressed on the second to last by default, es-TA-mus, and needs nothing; its a is slightly nasal only because an m follows it. Estão ends in ão, a default-last ending: the tilde makes the vowel nasal, and because no other accent is present, the tilde also marks the stress, es-TÃO, like English now said through the nose. In all of these the first syllable is weak: the e at the start of a word before s is often said i, and the s at the end of a syllable is s in São Paulo and sh in Rio, so estar can sound like is-TAR or esh-TAR.

Brazilians shorten estar in fast speech by dropping the weak first syllable: estou becomes tô, está becomes tá, estão becomes tão. What remains is one stressed syllable, and lesson 2 gave the rule for that: a stressed one-syllable word ending in a, e or o is written with an accent. So tá has an acute (open a) and tô a circumflex (closed o, like the o of go without the glide). The tilde of tão is the same as in estão.

Adjectives and professions show the other patterns. Simpático and médico are stressed on the third syllable from the end. No ending predicts that stress, so such words are always accented, and the vowel quality chooses the mark: open a and open e take the acute. The accent stays in simpática and médicas, because the stress stays on the same syllable. Alô is a-LÔ: it ends in o, so the default would be A-lo, and the stress on the last syllable needs a circumflex because the o is closed, exactly as in avô. Doente has two strong vowels side by side, o and e, and two strong vowels never make a diphthong, so it has three syllables, do-EN-te. Nasal vowels appear in cansado, doente, inteligente, estudante, engenheiro, enfermeira, onde, simpático, bem, quem, com, muito and não: whenever m or n closes a syllable, it is not said as a consonant but turns the vowel before it nasal. A tilde is written only on a and o, and only where no m or n does the job. In bem and quem the final em is said like ayn through the nose. Muito is a spelling exception: no tilde is written, but the m still nasalizes the diphthong ui.

The consonants follow the position rules. G before e is zh (inteligente, engenheiro), ç is s before a (engraçado), qu before e is k with a silent u (quem, que), nh is ny (engenheiro), h is silent (hoje, hospital), ss between vowels is s while a single s there is z (isso against casa), l at the end of a syllable is w (alto, mal, hospital, Rafael), t before an i sound is tch and d before an i sound is dj (triste, doente, estudante, onde, sede, médico). An unstressed final e counts as an i sound, which is why the t of triste and the d of onde change.

grammar.title: Ser and estar in the present: two verbs for to be
grammar.explanation:
English has one verb, to be, for every job: I am a teacher, I am tired, I am in Rio. Portuguese splits the work between two verbs, ser and estar. Spanish and Galician make the same split, so this is an ordinary feature of the Iberian languages, not a peculiarity of Portuguese. Both verbs are irregular, which in this course means they do not follow the stem plus ending pattern of a regular family, so each form is learned as it is. They are irregular because they are among the commonest verbs in the language, and the commonest words keep the oldest and most worn forms.

The split is old. Ser comes from two Latin verbs, esse (to be) and sedere (to sit). Estar comes from stare, to stand. The idea of standing explains what estar still does: it says that something is in a place or in a condition at some moment, as if it were standing there. Ser says what something is. That picture is not a rule, but it is the logic behind the rules in the next note.

The forms are few. In Brazil você, ele, ela and a gente share one form, because você is grammatically third person (lesson 3), and vocês, eles and elas share another. So each verb has four forms: sou, é, somos, são and estou, está, estamos, estão. Look at the stress. In a regular verb the stem carries the stress in these forms (FA-lo, FA-la, FA-lam), but in estou, está and estão the stress jumps to the ending: es-TOW, es-TÁ, es-TÃO. That jump is the irregularity, and the written accent on está and the tilde on estão record it. Estamos is es-TA-mus, with the stress where a regular verb would put it.

In everyday speech estar is shortened by dropping its weak first syllable: tô, tá, tão, and for we also tamos. English does the same with I'm, he's and they're. Tá is also used alone as okay, as in Tá bem or just Tá. Ser is not shortened in this way, and there is a reason: sou, é and são are already one syllable, and in somos the first syllable is the stressed one, so there is nothing weak to drop. Write the full forms when you write carefully, and expect to hear the short ones.

culture.title: Talking about how you feel in Brazil
culture.text:
When a Brazilian asks Tudo bem?, literally all well?, or Como você está?, the expected answer is usually short and positive: Tudo bem, Estou bem or just Tudo. But it is also normal to be honest about being tired, hungry or busy. People often say Tô cansado, with the shortened form of estou that you now know how to read, or Tô morrendo de fome, literally I am dying of hunger (morrendo is a verb form you will meet later; for now treat the whole phrase as one fixed expression), and another common answer is mais ou menos, literally more or less, meaning so-so. Brazilian conversation is warm, and sharing how you feel is a way to connect.

One word you will hear often is saudade, said sau-DA-dji. It describes missing someone or something, and there is no exact English translation. Estou com saudade de você means I miss you, and word for word it is I am with longing of you. It follows the same pattern as com fome and com sede: you are with the feeling, as a noun, so estar is the verb.

For professions, Brazilians often ask O que você faz?, literally what you do?, to find out someone's job (faz is a form of the verb fazer, to do or to make, which comes later; treat the question as a fixed formula for now), and you answer with ser and no article: Sou professor or Sou engenheira. Titles matter in some settings. Doutor and doutora are used for doctors and lawyers, and often for anyone in a professional role, even if the person does not have a doctorate. Professor and professora are also used as titles when speaking to a teacher directly, as in Bom dia, professora!

exercises.prompt: Why does está carry a written accent?
choices: It is stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default for a word ending in a
Two words have fused into one
It shows that the e is closed
exercises.explanation: A word ending in a is stressed on the second to last syllable by default (ES-ta). Está is stressed on the last syllable, so the stressed vowel is marked, with an acute because the a is open. Without the accent, esta means this.

exercises.prompt: In estão, what does the tilde do?
choices: It makes the vowel nasal and also marks the stressed syllable
It shows that the word is a contraction
exercises.explanation: The tilde nasalizes the vowel. When a word has no other accent, the tilde also marks the stress, so es-TÃO needs nothing more.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'I am tired' (said by a man)?
exercises.explanation: Tiredness is a condition, not a classification, so use estar, and a man uses the masculine cansado.
A profession classifies the person, so it takes ser, and eu takes sou.
Tiredness is a condition she is in, so estar, and ela takes está.
The place of a person takes estar, and nós takes estamos.

exercises.prompt: Match the Portuguese with the English
Which sentence can only be said by a woman?
exercises.explanation: Ocupada is an adjective, so it agrees with the speaker and takes the feminine -a. Bem is an adverb and fome is a noun, so neither changes, and Sou professor uses the masculine form.

exercises.prompt: Why is the plural of feliz written felizes and not felizs?
choices: A word ending in z takes a whole extra syllable, -es, in the plural
The z changes into an s
exercises.explanation: After z or r, the plural adds the syllable -es, because a z followed directly by s cannot be said. Words ending in a vowel add only -s.
Looking pretty on a particular day describes her condition at the moment, so estar. Ela é bonita would classify her as a pretty person.

exercises.hint_source: We are tired. (a group of women)
exercises.explanation: A gente means we but is grammatically singular, so the verb takes the form of ele and ela. Cansada agrees with the women in the group.
A condition takes estar, and a man uses the masculine cansado.
Não goes before the verb, a profession takes ser, and médica is feminine.
Hunger is expressed with estar com fome.

exercises.audio_target: Eu não sou médico, sou engenheiro.
exercises.hint_source: I am not a doctor, I am an engineer.

exercises.audio_target: Ela está em casa, mas está cansada.
exercises.hint_source: She is at home, but she is tired.
